scenes.headline: The evolution of money, in 9 stages
scenes.body: Barter. Shells. Coins. Paper. Banks. Cards. Crypto.
scenes.voiceover: The note in your wallet is just paper. So why will a shop give you bread for it? To answer that, we need to go back more than five thousand years.

scenes.headline: Barter and favours
scenes.voiceover: Stage one. Barter and favours.

scenes.headline: You need someone who wants what you have
scenes.voiceover: Imagine you have a goat and you need shoes. You'd have to find a shoemaker who also happens to want a goat, today. Economists call this the double coincidence of wants, and it's the problem money was invented to solve.
scenes.name: Barter and favours
scenes.body: Economists call it the double coincidence of wants.

scenes.headline: Most early communities ran on trust and IOUs
scenes.voiceover: But here's a twist. Anthropologists have found very few societies that ran purely on barter. In most villages, people gave each other things and kept track of who owed whom. Money began as a way of keeping score.
scenes.name: Barter and favours
scenes.body: Anthropologists have found few pure barter economies. Neighbours kept track of who owed whom.

scenes.headline: Commodity money
scenes.voiceover: Stage two. Commodity money.

scenes.headline: Cattle, grain, salt and shells
scenes.voiceover: The first money was made of things everyone already valued: cattle, grain, salt, and shells. Cowrie shells were used as money across Africa and Asia for thousands of years.

scenes.headline: The shekel: a weight of barley, then silver
scenes.voiceover: In ancient Mesopotamia, around three thousand BC, the shekel was a set weight of barley, and later of silver. Temples recorded debts in shekels on clay tablets. Some of the oldest writing we have is accounting.
scenes.name: Commodity money

scenes.headline: Cattle as wealth
scenes.voiceover: Closer to home, in many Southern African cultures, cattle were the main store of wealth, and they still carry that meaning today, in lobola.
scenes.name: Commodity money
scenes.body: In many Southern African cultures, cattle were, and still are, a store of wealth.

scenes.headline: Coins
scenes.voiceover: Stage three. Coins.

scenes.headline: The first official coins
scenes.voiceover: Around six hundred BC, the kingdom of Lydia, in today's Turkey, stamped lumps of electrum, a mix of gold and silver, with a royal seal. These were among the first official coins. The stamp meant you didn't have to weigh the metal. The king guaranteed it.
scenes.name: Coins

scenes.headline: Small, durable, countable, trusted
scenes.voiceover: At about the same time, China was using bronze coins shaped like tools. Coins spread because they were small, durable, easy to count, and backed by someone people trusted.

scenes.headline: Paper money
scenes.voiceover: Stage four. Paper money.

scenes.headline: From flying money to the first government banknotes
scenes.voiceover: Coins are heavy. In China, merchants began using paper receipts called flying money, and in ten twenty-four, the Song dynasty issued the first government paper money, the jiaozi.
scenes.name: Paper money

scenes.headline: Easy to print. Easy to over-print.
scenes.voiceover: Paper had a new danger. It's easy to print, and later Chinese governments printed too much of it. Prices soared and the notes lost their value, a story we covered in our video on currency collapses.
scenes.name: Paper money
scenes.body: Later Chinese dynasties printed too much, and the notes lost their value.

scenes.headline: Banks and banknotes
scenes.voiceover: Stage five. Banks and banknotes.

scenes.headline: A receipt for your gold becomes money
scenes.voiceover: In Europe, merchants left their gold with goldsmiths and bankers for safekeeping, and got a paper receipt. Soon people traded the receipts themselves, because they were easier to carry than gold.
scenes.name: Banks and banknotes

scenes.headline: Europe's first banknotes
scenes.voiceover: In sixteen sixty-one, Stockholms Banco in Sweden issued Europe's first banknotes. It printed more notes than it could back, and within a few years it collapsed.
scenes.name: Banks and banknotes

scenes.headline: Central banks
scenes.voiceover: Stage six. Central banks.

scenes.headline: The Riksbank: the world's oldest central bank
scenes.voiceover: That collapse led Sweden to create the Riksbank in sixteen sixty-eight, the oldest central bank still operating. England followed with the Bank of England in sixteen ninety-four, set up to lend the government money for war.
scenes.name: Central banks

scenes.headline: The South African Reserve Bank
scenes.voiceover: The United States created the Federal Reserve in nineteen thirteen, and the South African Reserve Bank opened in nineteen twenty-one. Today it alone issues our banknotes and coins.
scenes.name: Central banks

scenes.headline: Issues the currency. Sets interest rates. Rescues the system.
scenes.voiceover: Central banks do three big things. They issue the currency, they set interest rates, like the repo rate, and they act as lender of last resort when banks get into trouble. Their main job is to keep prices stable, so your money holds its value.
scenes.body: Its main job: keep prices stable, so your rand holds its value.

scenes.headline: The gold standard, briefly
scenes.voiceover: Stage seven. The gold standard.

scenes.headline: Notes you could swap for gold
scenes.voiceover: For about a century, many currencies were tied to gold. In theory, you could swap your notes for a fixed amount of it. Gold mined right here in South Africa helped keep that system running.

scenes.headline: 1971: the dollar cuts its link to gold
scenes.voiceover: But the link was hard to keep. In nineteen seventy-one, the United States stopped swapping dollars for gold, and the world moved to fiat money: money that's valuable because governments declare it so, and people trust it.
scenes.name: The gold standard

stat.label: End of dollar convertibility to gold

scenes.headline: Cards and electronic money
scenes.voiceover: Stage eight. Cards and electronic money.

scenes.headline: Cards, ATMs and electronic transfers
scenes.voiceover: In nineteen fifty, Diners Club launched one of the first charge cards. The first cash machine opened in London in nineteen sixty-seven. Money slowly became numbers in a bank's computer.

scenes.headline: M-Pesa: money on a basic phone
scenes.voiceover: Africa leapfrogged. In two thousand and seven, Kenya's M-Pesa let people send money by text message, without a bank account. And in South Africa, PayShap now lets you pay instantly using just a phone number.
scenes.name: Cards and electronic money

scenes.headline: Digital currencies
scenes.voiceover: Stage nine. Digital currencies.

scenes.headline: Money with no central bank
scenes.voiceover: In two thousand and nine, someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin, digital money with no central bank and a fixed supply, recorded on a public ledger called a blockchain. Thousands of cryptocurrencies followed, along with stablecoins tied to the dollar.

scenes.headline: Digital versions of national money
scenes.voiceover: Central banks are responding with digital versions of their own money. The Bahamas launched the Sand Dollar in twenty twenty, Nigeria launched the eNaira in twenty twenty-one, and China is piloting a digital yuan. Our own Reserve Bank has tested the technology through Project Khokha.
scenes.name: Digital currencies
scenes.body: The Bahamas' Sand Dollar (2020), Nigeria's eNaira (2021), China's e-CNY pilots, and the SARB's Project Khokha trials.

scenes.headline: Money has always been about trust.
scenes.voiceover: Cattle, shells, coins, paper, plastic, code. The form keeps changing, but the idea doesn't. Money works because we trust that someone else will accept it tomorrow. When that trust breaks, money fails.

scenes.headline: Will cash still exist in 20 years?
scenes.voiceover: So what's next? Will you still carry cash in twenty years? Tell us in the comments.

endcard.title: Money is trust
endcard.subtitle: Subscribe for South African money, explained.
